definition: The Andean creator, said to have risen from Lake Titicaca and made the sun, moon, stars and peoples. Colonial chronicles describe him in different ways, and his name was also applied to the Spaniards.

The earth understood as a living mother in Quechua and Aymara communities. She receives daily offerings of chicha and food, and larger despacho bundles, in return for fertility, health and protection.

A named mountain understood as a powerful being with its own territory and temperament. Apus send water and weather, and receive offerings; the greatest, such as Ausangate, are honoured far beyond their valleys.
A culture of Peru's north coast, roughly 100 to 700 CE, known for painted ceramics, adobe pyramids and elaborate burials. Moche art shows ritual sacrifice, but the society left no written texts.
A province in the highlands above Lima, and the Quechua manuscript of about 1608 that records its gods, shrines and stories. It was compiled under the priest Francisco de Ávila.
The Andean kin group or community that held land and labour in common and honoured its own ancestors and shrines. Ayllus still exist, and membership carries rights and obligations.
A rotating labour obligation in the Inka state, by which communities supplied workers for roads, mines, fields and building projects. The Spanish adapted it into a harsh system of forced labour.
A record made of knotted cords, used in the Inka state for accounting, tribute and possibly narrative. The code is not fully deciphered, so much of what quipus recorded remains uncertain.
The Inka king of a modern Quechua millenarian story. Beheaded by the Spaniards, his head grows a new body underground, and when it is complete he will return and restore the world.
The high lake on the Peru-Bolivia border, central to Andean creation stories. Viracocha is said to have risen from it, and the islands of the Sun and Moon are among its shrines.
